podcast.title: Top of the Pops Performance (July 6, 1972)
podcast.body: As guitarist for The Spiders from Mars, Mick Ronson performed with David Bowie on Top of the Pops on July 6, 1972, wearing a gold one-piece costume. His relaxed demeanor and the public display of affection from Bowie (an arm draped around his shoulders) were notable and impactful. "Onstage with him was his guitarist, Mick Ronson, dressed in a gold one piece."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Death (April 1993)
podcast.body: Mick Ronson, who was David Bowie's guitarist and Morrissey's producer, died in April 1993 from cancer. "Mick Ronson, David Bowie's guitarist and Morrissey's producer, Cancer April 1993."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Co-production of Lou Reed's "Transformer"
podcast.body: Mick Ronson, known as the guitarist who worked with David Bowie, collaborated with Bowie to produce Lou Reed's influential album "Transformer." Ronson had traveled with Bowie to contact Lou Reed regarding the project. "El disco salió gracias al dinero de David Bowie y fue producido por el propio David Bowie y por Mik Ronson, que era el guitarrista que trabajaba con David Bowie que se había ido con él a contactar con Luric."

srcs.episode: Tras los pasos de Lou Reed

podcast.title: Collaboration with David Bowie
podcast.body: As David Bowie's Spiders From Mars guitarist, Mick Ronson collaborated with Bowie to produce Lou Reed's 1972 album, *Transformer*. Their work helped Reed find a new sound, demonstrating Ronson's influence beyond his guitar playing. "Bowie and his spiders from Mars guitarist, Mick Ronson, helped Lou find a new sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Top of the Pops Performance (July 6, 1972)
xref.body: Bowie's seminal performance on Top of the Pops on July 6, 1972, with The Spiders from Mars, was highly influential. Dressed in a quilted jumpsuit, red boxing boots with green laces, and bright red-orange hair, Bowie's anisocoria (permanently dilated pupil from a childhood fight) added to his "otherworldly look." His public display of affection towards guitarist Mick Ronson (draping his arm around his shoulders) was considered "super duper gay" for the era and had a profound impact, leading to the immediate appearance of "Ziggy Clones" and helping young people feel accepted in their sexuality. "One especially interesting performance was on top of the pops on the BBC, July 6th, 1972."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Correct Pronunciation of "Bowie"
xref.body: The correct pronunciation of his adopted surname is "Bowie," not "Bowie" or "Bow-ee." Bowie himself affirmed this pronunciation, despite guitarist Mick Ronson and others sometimes mispronouncing it. "It should be pronounced Bowie. And trust me, I spoke to the man himself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Patronage of Lou Reed
xref.body: Bowie was also a great admirer of Lou Reed and The Velvet Underground, recognizing Reed's talent despite him being on the fringes and largely unknown. Bowie offered his patronage, leading him to produce Reed's 1972 album *Transformer*, collaborating with his Spiders From Mars guitarist, Mick Ronson, to help Reed find a new sound. "Bowie did, though, and he offered to lend his patronage to Lou."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Ziggy Stardust Character's Impact
xref.body: Bowie's Ziggy Stardust character offered significant hope to many, presenting himself as a weirdly androgynous, potentially bisexual figure who wore makeup and glitter and performed provocative acts on stage, such as simulating oral sex with his guitarist, Mick Ronson. Despite Bowie himself not being 100% gay, the character's persona profoundly impacted and inspired closeted people worldwide. "Ziggy was this weirdly androgynous, maybe bisexual creature who wore makeup and glitter and did all kinds of looed things on stage, like simulating oral sex in his guitarist, Mick Ronson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
